prompt: Why is it important to consider accessibility when choosing colors for a website?
options: Accessible colors are more visually appealing.
Accessible colors ensure that content is readable by all users, including those with visual impairments.
Accessible colors make the website load faster.
Accessible colors are easier to implement with CSS.
correctAnswer: Accessible colors ensure that content is readable by all users, including those with visual impairments.
explanation: Color contrast is a key factor in web accessibility.

prompt: Which CSS property is used to change the font of an element?
correctAnswer: `font-family`
explanation: `font-family` specifies the font for an element.

prompt: Which CSS property controls the size of the text?
correctAnswer: `font-size`
explanation: `font-size` sets the size of the font.

prompt: How can you make text bold using CSS?
correctAnswer: `font-weight: bold;`
explanation: `font-weight` controls the boldness of text.

prompt: Which CSS property is used to align text horizontally (e.g., left, center, right)?
correctAnswer: `text-align`
explanation: `text-align` sets the horizontal alignment of text.

prompt: Which CSS property is used to add or remove underlines from text?
correctAnswer: `text-decoration`
explanation: `text-decoration` can set `underline`, `overline`, `line-through`, or `none`.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when setting `font-size` in CSS?
options: Using pixel values exclusively, limiting user scalability.
correctAnswer: Using pixel values exclusively, limiting user scalability.
explanation: Relative units like `em` or `rem` are better for accessibility.

prompt: Which CSS property controls the spacing between lines of text?
correctAnswer: `line-height`
explanation: `line-height` sets the height of a line of text.

prompt: How can you make text uppercase using CSS?
correctAnswer: `text-transform: uppercase;`
explanation: `text-transform` changes the capitalization of text.

prompt: Which CSS property is used to indent the first line of text in a block?
correctAnswer: `text-indent`
explanation: `text-indent` indents the first line of text.

prompt: Why is it important to consider `line-height` for readability?
options: A larger `line-height` makes text appear smaller.
Appropriate `line-height` improves the visual separation of lines, making text easier to read.
`line-height` is primarily for vertical alignment of elements.
correctAnswer: Appropriate `line-height` improves the visual separation of lines, making text easier to read.
explanation: Good line spacing prevents text from feeling cramped.

prompt: Which `display` value causes an element to start on a new line and take up the full available width?
correctAnswer: `block`
explanation: Block-level elements behave this way.

prompt: Which `display` value causes an element to sit on the same line as surrounding content and only take up necessary width?
correctAnswer: `inline`
explanation: Inline elements do not force a new line.

prompt: Which `display` value allows an element to sit on the same line as others, but also allows setting width and height?
correctAnswer: `inline-block`
explanation: `inline-block` offers a hybrid behavior.

prompt: Which of the following HTML elements is typically a block-level element by default?
correctAnswer: `<div>`
explanation: `<div>` is a common block-level container.

prompt: Which of the following HTML elements is typically an inline element by default?
correctAnswer: `<span>`
explanation: `<span>` is a generic inline container.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when using the `display` property?
options: Trying to apply `width` or `height` to an `inline` element.
correctAnswer: Trying to apply `width` or `height` to an `inline` element.
explanation: `width` and `height` properties do not affect inline elements.

prompt: If you set `display: none;` on an element, what happens to it?
options: It becomes invisible but still takes up space.
It is completely removed from the document flow and is not rendered.
correctAnswer: It is completely removed from the document flow and is not rendered.
explanation: `display: none;` hides the element entirely.

prompt: To center a block-level element horizontally on a page, what CSS properties would you typically use?
correctAnswer: `margin: auto;` (with a defined width)
explanation: `margin: auto;` on left and right centers a block element with a set width.

prompt: Which `display` value is often used to create flexible and responsive layouts?
correctAnswer: `flex`
explanation: `display: flex;` is key for Flexbox layouts.

prompt: Why is understanding the difference between `block` and `inline` elements crucial for layout?
options: It affects the font size of the text.
It determines how elements interact with each other in terms of space and flow.
It changes the color of the elements.
It is only relevant for mobile devices.
correctAnswer: It determines how elements interact with each other in terms of space and flow.
explanation: It dictates how elements occupy space and break lines.

prompt: What is the default value of the `position` property in CSS?
correctAnswer: `static`
explanation: Elements are positioned according to the normal flow by default.

prompt: Which `position` value allows you to move an element relative to its normal position, leaving a gap where it would have been?
correctAnswer: `relative`
explanation: `relative` positioning shifts an element from its original spot.

prompt: Which `position` value removes an element from the normal document flow and positions it relative to its nearest *positioned* ancestor?
correctAnswer: `absolute`
explanation: `absolute` elements are positioned relative to a non-static parent.

prompt: Which `position` value keeps an element in the same place on the screen, even when the user scrolls?
correctAnswer: `fixed`
explanation: `fixed` elements are positioned relative to the viewport.

prompt: What happens if you apply `top: 20px;` to an element with `position: static;`?
correctAnswer: Nothing happens.
explanation: `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` only work with non-static positioning.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when using CSS positioning?
options: Forgetting to set a `position` value other than `static` before using `top`, `left`, etc.
Using `position: fixed;` for elements that should scroll.
correctAnswer: Forgetting to set a `position` value other than `static` before using `top`, `left`, etc.
explanation: This is a fundamental concept for positioning to work.

prompt: If an absolutely positioned element has no positioned ancestors, where will it be positioned relative to?
correctAnswer: The `<body>` element
explanation: It defaults to the initial containing block, which is the `<body>`.

prompt: Which property controls the stacking order of positioned elements (which element appears on top)?
correctAnswer: `z-index`
explanation: `z-index` specifies the stack order of an element.

prompt: Which `position` value behaves like `relative` until a certain scroll point, then becomes `fixed`?
correctAnswer: `sticky`
explanation: `sticky` elements toggle between relative and fixed.

prompt: Why is understanding `position: absolute;` and its relationship with `position: relative;` on parent elements important?
options: It allows for precise placement of child elements within a specific parent container.
It is only used for responsive design.
correctAnswer: It allows for precise placement of child elements within a specific parent container.
explanation: `relative` on parent creates a positioning context for `absolute` children.

prompt: What CSS property is used to enable Flexbox on a container?
correctAnswer: `display: flex;`
explanation: `display: flex;` turns an element into a flex container.

prompt: What are the direct children of a flex container called?
correctAnswer: Flex items
explanation: Direct children become flex items.

prompt: Which property defines the direction flex items are placed in the flex container?
correctAnswer: `flex-direction`
explanation: `flex-direction` can be `row`, `row-reverse`, `column`, `column-reverse`.

prompt: How can you center flex items horizontally within a flex container?
correctAnswer: `justify-content: center;`
explanation: `justify-content` aligns items along the main axis.

prompt: How can you center flex items vertically within a flex container?
correctAnswer: `align-items: center;`
explanation: `align-items` aligns items along the cross axis.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when using Flexbox?
options: Forgetting to set `display: flex;` on the parent container.
correctAnswer: Forgetting to set `display: flex;` on the parent container.
explanation: The parent must be a flex container for flex properties to work.

prompt: Which property allows flex items to wrap onto multiple lines if there isn't enough space?
correctAnswer: `flex-wrap`
explanation: `flex-wrap` controls whether flex items are forced onto one line or can wrap.

prompt: Which property is a shorthand for `flex-direction` and `flex-wrap`?
correctAnswer: `flex-flow`
explanation: `flex-flow` combines these two properties.

prompt: If you want flex items to take up equal available space, which property would you apply to the flex items?
correctAnswer: `flex-grow: 1;`
explanation: `flex-grow` specifies how much a flex item will grow relative to the rest of the flex items.

prompt: Why is Flexbox considered a powerful tool for responsive web design?
options: It provides a flexible and efficient way to lay out, align, and distribute space among items in a container, adapting to different screen sizes.
It only works on mobile devices.
It replaces the need for media queries.
correctAnswer: It provides a flexible and efficient way to lay out, align, and distribute space among items in a container, adapting to different screen sizes.
explanation: Flexbox simplifies creating adaptable layouts.

prompt: What CSS property is used to enable Grid Layout on a container?
correctAnswer: `display: grid;`
explanation: `display: grid;` turns an element into a grid container.

prompt: CSS Grid is primarily a _________ layout system.
correctAnswer: Two-dimensional
explanation: Grid allows control over both rows and columns.

prompt: Which property defines the number and size of columns in a grid layout?
correctAnswer: `grid-template-columns`
explanation: `grid-template-columns` defines the column tracks.

prompt: Which property defines the number and size of rows in a grid layout?
correctAnswer: `grid-template-rows`
explanation: `grid-template-rows` defines the row tracks.

prompt: What unit in CSS Grid represents a fraction of the available space?
correctAnswer: `fr`
explanation: The `fr` unit distributes available space proportionally.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when learning CSS Grid?
correctAnswer: Confusing its purpose with Flexbox.
explanation: Grid is for 2D layouts, Flexbox for 1D.

prompt: How can you place a grid item to start at column line 2 and end at column line 4?
options: Both a and b are correct.
correctAnswer: `grid-column: 2 / 4;`
explanation: Both are valid ways to specify grid item placement.

prompt: Which property is used to define the gap between grid rows and columns?
options: Both b and c are correct.
correctAnswer: `grid-gap`
explanation: `grid-gap` is the older syntax, `gap` is the modern shorthand.

prompt: If you define `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr;`, how will the three columns be sized?
options: All three columns will be of equal width.
The first and third columns will be equal, and the second will be twice as wide.
The first column will be the widest, and the third the narrowest.
The columns will have fixed widths.
correctAnswer: The first and third columns will be equal, and the second will be twice as wide.
explanation: `fr` units distribute space proportionally.

prompt: Why is CSS Grid considered a powerful tool for overall page layout?
options: It only works for simple, single-column designs.
It provides a robust and intuitive way to create complex, responsive two-dimensional layouts for entire web pages.
It replaces the need for all other CSS properties.
It is only useful for small components, not full pages.
correctAnswer: It provides a robust and intuitive way to create complex, responsive two-dimensional layouts for entire web pages.
explanation: Grid is ideal for defining the main structure of a page.

prompt: What is the primary goal of responsive web design?
options: To ensure websites look and function well on all devices and screen sizes.
To use only CSS Grid for layout.
To eliminate the need for JavaScript.
correctAnswer: To ensure websites look and function well on all devices and screen sizes.
explanation: Responsive design adapts to the user's environment.

prompt: Which CSS feature is essential for creating responsive layouts based on screen size?
correctAnswer: Media Queries
explanation: Media queries apply styles conditionally based on device characteristics.

prompt: What is the syntax for defining a media query in CSS?
correctAnswer: `@media`
explanation: The `@media` rule introduces a media query.

prompt: If you want a style to apply only when the screen width is 600 pixels or less, which media query would you use?
correctAnswer: `@media (max-width: 600px)`
explanation: `max-width` targets screens up to that size.

prompt: If you want a style to apply only when the screen width is 768 pixels or more, which media query would you use?
correctAnswer: `@media (min-width: 768px)`
explanation: `min-width` targets screens from that size upwards.

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when approaching responsive design?
options: Designing for desktop first and struggling to adapt it for mobile later.
correctAnswer: Designing for desktop first and struggling to adapt it for mobile later.
explanation: A "mobile-first" approach is generally recommended.

prompt: What does the "mobile-first" approach mean in responsive design?
options: Designing the website only for mobile devices.
Writing CSS for small screens first, then using `min-width` media queries to add styles for larger screens.
Writing CSS for large screens first, then using `max-width` media queries for smaller screens.
Using JavaScript to detect mobile devices.
correctAnswer: Writing CSS for small screens first, then using `min-width` media queries to add styles for larger screens.
explanation: It prioritizes the core content and layout for smaller screens.

prompt: Which HTML tag is crucial for responsive design to ensure the browser scales the page correctly on mobile devices?
correctAnswer: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`
explanation: The viewport meta tag controls layout on mobile browsers.

prompt: Can media queries be used to detect device orientation (portrait vs. landscape)?
options: No, media queries only detect width and height.
correctAnswer: Yes, using `@media (orientation: portrait)` or `@media (orientation: landscape)`.
explanation: Media queries can check various device features, including orientation.

prompt: Why are media queries important for modern web development?
options: They allow a single HTML document to provide an optimal viewing experience across a wide range of devices.
They replace the need for HTML structure.
correctAnswer: They allow a single HTML document to provide an optimal viewing experience across a wide range of devices.
explanation: They are the foundation of adaptable, responsive layouts.

prompt: Which `display` property value causes an element to take up the full width available and start on a new line?
correctAnswer: `block`
explanation: Elements with `display: block;` behave like paragraphs, pushing subsequent content to a new line and taking all available horizontal space.*

prompt: What is a key characteristic of an element with `display: inline;`?
options: It can have its `width` and `height` explicitly set.
It always starts on a new line.
It only takes up as much width as its content requires.
It can contain other block-level elements.
correctAnswer: It only takes up as much width as its content requires.
explanation: Inline elements are designed to flow with text and only occupy the space needed for their content, ignoring explicit width/height settings.*

prompt: Consider the following CSS: `div { display: inline; width: 200px; }`. What will be the actual width of the `div` element?
options: The full width of its parent container
correctAnswer: The width of its content
explanation: `width` and `height` properties do not apply to elements with `display: inline;`. The `div` will only be as wide as its content.*

prompt: Which `display` value allows an element to behave like an `inline` element but also accept `width` and `height` properties?
correctAnswer: `inline-block`
explanation: `inline-block` elements flow inline with text but can have dimensions (width, height, padding, margin) applied, making them versatile for layout.*

prompt: A web developer wants to hide an element completely from the page, making it occupy no space and be inaccessible to screen readers. Which `display` value should be used?
correctAnswer: `none`
explanation: `display: none;` removes the element from the document flow entirely, making it invisible and non-interactive.*

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when working with `display: inline;` elements?
correctAnswer: Expecting `width` and `height` properties to apply.
explanation: A frequent error is attempting to size inline elements with `width` or `height`, which are ignored by the browser for `inline` elements.*

prompt: You have a navigation menu where list items (`<li>`) need to appear side-by-side. Which `display` property is most suitable for the `<li>` elements?
correctAnswer: `display: inline;` or `display: inline-block;`
explanation: Both `inline` and `inline-block` allow elements to sit next to each other. `inline-block` is often preferred for navigation items as it allows for setting padding and margins more predictably.*

prompt: Which `display` value is typically used on a parent container to enable a one-dimensional layout system for its direct children?
correctAnswer: `display: flex;`
explanation: `display: flex;` turns an element into a flex container, allowing its direct children (flex items) to be laid out and aligned along a single axis.*

prompt: When debugging layout issues, you notice an element is taking up more space than expected horizontally, pushing other elements down. Which `display` property value is the most likely cause?
correctAnswer: `display: block;`
explanation: `display: block;` elements by default take up 100% of the available width, which can cause them to push subsequent content to a new line.*

prompt: To create a simple row of social media icons that are evenly spaced and vertically centered, which `display` property would you apply to their parent container?
correctAnswer: `display: flex;`
explanation: `display: flex;` on the parent container allows for easy alignment and distribution of child items (the icons) along a single axis, making it ideal for such a layout.*

prompt: What is the default value of the `box-sizing` property in CSS?
correctAnswer: `content-box`
explanation: By default, `width` and `height` refer only to the content area, and padding/border are added outside.*

prompt: When `box-sizing` is set to `content-box`, what does a `width` of `100px` refer to?
options: The total width of the element, including padding and border.
The width of the content area only.
The width of the padding and content combined.
The width of the border and content combined.
correctAnswer: The width of the content area only.
explanation: In `content-box` mode, `width` and `height` explicitly define the dimensions of the content area.*

prompt: If an element has `width: 200px; padding: 10px; border: 5px solid black;` and `box-sizing: content-box;`, what will be its total rendered width?
explanation: `200px` (content) + `10px` (left padding) + `10px` (right padding) + `5px` (left border) + `5px` (right border) = `230px`.*

prompt: Which `box-sizing` value makes layout calculations more intuitive by including padding and border within the specified `width` and `height`?
correctAnswer: `border-box`
explanation: With `border-box`, the `width` and `height` properties define the outer dimensions of the element, including padding and border.*

prompt: A developer sets `width: 150px; padding: 20px;` on an element with `box-sizing: border-box;`. What is the width of the content area?
explanation: `150px` (total width) - `20px` (left padding) - `20px` (right padding) = `110px` content width.*

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake related to `box-sizing`?
options: Forgetting that `border-box` includes margin in its calculation.
Not accounting for padding and border when using `content-box`, leading to layout shifts.
Using `box-sizing` on elements that don't have a `width` or `height`.
correctAnswer: Not accounting for padding and border when using `content-box`, leading to layout shifts.
explanation: Beginners often overlook that padding and border add to the total size in `content-box` mode, causing elements to be larger than intended.*

prompt: You are creating a grid of items, and you want each item to have a `width` of `33.33%` and `10px` of padding without affecting the total `33.33%` width. Which `box-sizing` value should you use?
correctAnswer: `border-box`
explanation: `border-box` ensures that the `10px` padding is included within the `33.33%` width, preventing the items from exceeding their allocated space.*

prompt: Why do many modern CSS resets and frameworks include `html { box-sizing: border-box; } , ::before, *::after { box-sizing: inherit; }`?
options: To ensure consistent box model behavior across all elements and make layout easier.
To make elements responsive by default.
correctAnswer: To ensure consistent box model behavior across all elements and make layout easier.
explanation: This global setting simplifies layout calculations by making `width` and `height` consistently include padding and border for all elements.*

prompt: If you have two `div` elements side-by-side, each with `width: 50%;` and `box-sizing: content-box;`, and you add `padding: 5px;` to both, what will likely happen?
options: They will remain side-by-side, but their content area will shrink.
One of the `div`s will drop to the next line.
Their total width will still be `50%` each.
correctAnswer: One of the `div`s will drop to the next line.
explanation: The `5px` padding will be added *outside* the `50%` width, making each `div` wider than `50%`, thus forcing one to wrap to the next line.*

prompt: When building a component with a fixed `width` and `height` that needs internal spacing, which `box-sizing` value is generally preferred for easier calculation of the content area?
correctAnswer: `border-box`
explanation: With `border-box`, you set the total dimensions, and any padding or border you add will reduce the content area, making it straightforward to manage the component's overall size.*

prompt: Which CSS property creates space inside an element, between its content and its border?
correctAnswer: `padding`
explanation: Padding adds space within the element, effectively increasing the area between the content and the element's border.*

prompt: Which CSS property creates space outside an element, between its border and adjacent elements?
correctAnswer: `margin`
explanation: Margin creates external space, pushing elements away from each other.*

prompt: If an element has `padding: 20px;`, what does this mean?
options: It has 20px of space outside its border on all sides.
It has 20px of space between its content and border on all sides.
correctAnswer: It has 20px of space between its content and border on all sides.
explanation: `padding` adds internal space between the content and the element's inner edge.*

prompt: Consider a `div` with `margin-top: 15px;`. What effect will this have?
options: It will add 15px of space above the `div`'s content.
It will add 15px of space inside the `div`'s top edge.
It will add 15px of space between the `div`'s top border and the element above it.
It will make the `div`'s top border 15px thick.
correctAnswer: It will add 15px of space between the `div`'s top border and the element above it.
explanation: `margin-top` creates external space above the element, pushing it away from the element above.*

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when using `margin` and `padding`?
options: Confusing their roles and applying them incorrectly for internal vs. external spacing.
correctAnswer: Confusing their roles and applying them incorrectly for internal vs. external spacing.
explanation: A frequent error is misunderstanding whether to use `margin` for external spacing or `padding` for internal spacing.*

prompt: You want to increase the clickable area of a button without changing its text size or making it appear further from other elements. Which property should you adjust?
correctAnswer: `padding`
explanation: Padding increases the internal space, making the button larger and its clickable area bigger, without affecting its external spacing.*

prompt: To create visual separation between two adjacent `div` elements, which property would you primarily use on one or both of them?
correctAnswer: `margin`
explanation: Margin creates space *between* elements, effectively separating them visually.*

prompt: If you have a `div` with `background-color: lightblue;` and you apply `padding: 10px;` and `margin: 20px;`, which area will be `lightblue`?
options: The content area plus the padding.
The content area, padding, and margin.
correctAnswer: The content area plus the padding.
explanation: The background color extends to cover the content and padding areas, but not the margin.*

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a valid way to specify `padding`?
correctAnswer: `padding: 10;`
explanation: `padding` requires a unit (e.g., `px`, `em`, `%`) after the numerical value.*

prompt: You are designing a card component. You want the text inside the card to have some breathing room from the card's edges, and you want the card itself to be spaced out from other cards. Which properties would you use for these two distinct spacing needs?
options: `margin` for internal space, `padding` for external space.
`padding` for internal space, `margin` for external space.
`border` for internal space, `outline` for external space.
`gap` for internal space, `spacing` for external space.
correctAnswer: `padding` for internal space, `margin` for external space.
explanation: Padding provides internal spacing for the text within the card, while margin provides external spacing to separate cards from each other.*

prompt: Which CSS property is part of the element's box model and takes up space in the document flow?
correctAnswer: `border`
explanation: The border is an integral part of the box model, affecting the element's dimensions and layout.*

prompt: Which CSS property is drawn outside the element's border and does NOT take up space in the document flow?
correctAnswer: `outline`
explanation: Outlines are purely visual and do not influence the layout of other elements.*

prompt: You want to add a 1-pixel dashed red line around an image that should not affect the surrounding content's position. Which property should you use?
correctAnswer: `outline: 1px dashed red;`
explanation: An outline will draw the line without altering the document flow, preserving the layout.*

prompt: What is the primary purpose of the `outline` property in terms of user experience?
options: To add decorative styling to elements.
To create extra spacing around elements.
To indicate focus for accessibility, especially for keyboard users.
To define the clickable area of an element.
correctAnswer: To indicate focus for accessibility, especially for keyboard users.
explanation: Outlines are crucial for visual feedback, showing users which element is currently focused.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake is removing the default `outline` on interactive elements. Why is this considered bad practice?
options: It makes the website load slower.
It can cause layout shifts when elements are focused.
It significantly harms accessibility for keyboard and assistive technology users.
It prevents hover effects from working correctly.
correctAnswer: It significantly harms accessibility for keyboard and assistive technology users.
explanation: Removing outlines makes it difficult for users who navigate with a keyboard to see which element they are interacting with.*

prompt: Which of the following `border` properties is used to set the style of the border (e.g., solid, dashed, dotted)?
correctAnswer: `border-style`
explanation: `border-style` determines the visual appearance of the border line.*

prompt: You have a button and you want to give it a rounded border. Which CSS property would you use in conjunction with `border`?
correctAnswer: `border-radius`
explanation: `border-radius` allows you to round the corners of an element's border.*

prompt: Consider an element with `border: 5px solid green;` and `outline: 2px dotted purple;`. Which line will appear closer to the element's content?
options: Neither, as outlines are ignored if a border is present.
correctAnswer: The green solid border.
explanation: The border is inside the outline, closer to the padding and content.*

prompt: Which CSS shorthand property allows you to set the `border-width`, `border-style`, and `border-color` in a single declaration?
correctAnswer: `border`
explanation: The `border` shorthand property is commonly used for this purpose.*

prompt: When designing a custom focus indicator for an interactive element, which property should you primarily modify to ensure accessibility without disrupting layout?
correctAnswer: `outline`
explanation: Modifying the `outline` is the standard and most accessible way to create custom focus indicators without affecting the page's layout.*

prompt: What is margin collapse in CSS?
options: When horizontal margins of adjacent elements combine.
When vertical margins of adjacent block-level elements combine into a single margin.
When padding and margin values are equal.
When an element's margin is set to zero.
correctAnswer: When vertical margins of adjacent block-level elements combine into a single margin.
explanation: Margin collapse specifically refers to the merging of vertical margins between certain block-level elements.*

prompt: Which type of margins are affected by margin collapse?
correctAnswer: Only vertical margins (top and bottom).
explanation: Margin collapse is a behavior exclusive to vertical margins.*

prompt: If `div A` has `margin-bottom: 20px;` and `div B` immediately below it has `margin-top: 30px;`, what will be the effective vertical space between them due to margin collapse?
explanation: The larger of the two collapsing margins (30px) will be used.*

prompt: Which of the following scenarios can cause margin collapse?
options: Two `inline` elements next to each other.
A parent `div` with `padding-top: 1px;` and its first child `p` with `margin-top: 20px;`.
Two `flex` items within a flex container.
correctAnswer: An empty `div` with `margin-top: 10px;` and `margin-bottom: 15px;`.
explanation: An empty block with only vertical margins will collapse its own top and bottom margins.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake is being surprised by unexpected vertical spacing between elements. What is the most likely CSS phenomenon causing this?
correctAnswer: Margin collapse.
explanation: Margin collapse often leads to less vertical space than expected if margins were assumed to add up.*

prompt: Which CSS property, when applied to a parent element, can prevent its top margin from collapsing with its first child's top margin?
correctAnswer: Both `padding-top` and `border-top`.
explanation: Adding any padding or border between the parent and child prevents their margins from collapsing.*

prompt: You have a `div` with `margin-top: 40px;` and `margin-bottom: 40px;` but no content, padding, or border. What will be the effective vertical margin for this empty `div`?
explanation: The top and bottom margins of an empty block collapse with each other, resulting in a single margin equal to the larger of the two.*

prompt: Which of the following layout methods inherently prevents margin collapse between its direct children?
correctAnswer: `display: flex;`
explanation: Flex items within a flex container do not experience margin collapse.*

prompt: To ensure that the top margin of a parent element does not collapse with the top margin of its first child, which CSS declaration could you add to the parent?
correctAnswer: `overflow: hidden;`
explanation: Setting `overflow: hidden;` (or any value other than `visible`) on the parent creates a new block formatting context, preventing margin collapse.*

prompt: You are styling a series of headings (`<h2>`, `<h3>`) and want consistent vertical spacing between them, regardless of their individual top/bottom margins. What CSS approach would be most reliable to achieve this without margin collapse?

Wrap each heading in a `div` with `overflow: hidden;`.

prompt: What is the default value of the `position` property for all HTML elements?
correctAnswer: `static`
explanation: Elements with `position: static;` are rendered in the normal document flow.*

prompt: Which `position` value allows an element to be offset from its normal position while still occupying its original space in the document flow?
correctAnswer: `relative`
explanation: `position: relative;` offsets an element from its original position, but its original space is preserved.*

prompt: An element with `position: absolute;` is positioned relative to which element by default?
options: The `<html>` element (initial containing block) if no positioned ancestor exists.
correctAnswer: The `<html>` element (initial containing block) if no positioned ancestor exists.
explanation: If no parent has a `position` other than `static`, `absolute` elements position relative to the initial containing block.*

prompt: Which `position` value removes an element from the normal document flow and keeps it in the same place on the screen even when the user scrolls?
correctAnswer: `fixed`
explanation: `position: fixed;` elements are positioned relative to the viewport and remain stationary during scrolling.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake when using `position: absolute;` is forgetting to set which property on its parent container?
correctAnswer: `position: relative;` (or `absolute`, `fixed`, `sticky`)
explanation: Without a positioned ancestor, an `absolute` element will position relative to the `<html>` element, often leading to unexpected placement.*

prompt: You want to create a tooltip that appears directly next to an icon when hovered. The tooltip should be positioned relative to the icon. Which `position` value should the icon have, and which should the tooltip have?
correctAnswer: Icon: `relative`, Tooltip: `absolute`
explanation: Setting the icon to `relative` makes it a positioning context for the `absolute` tooltip, allowing the tooltip to be placed precisely next to it.*

prompt: Which `position` value behaves like `relative` until the element scrolls to a certain threshold, after which it becomes `fixed`?
correctAnswer: `sticky`
explanation: `position: sticky;` is often used for navigation headers that stick to the top of the viewport after scrolling past them.*

prompt: If an element has `position: relative; top: 20px; left: 30px;`, what does `top: 20px;` mean?
options: The element will be 20px from the top of the viewport.
The element will be 20px from the top of its parent.
The element will be 20px down from its original static position.
The element will be 20px from the top of the document.
correctAnswer: The element will be 20px down from its original static position.
explanation: `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` for `relative` positioning offset the element from where it *would have been* in the normal flow.*

prompt: When an element is `position: absolute;`, what happens to the space it originally occupied in the document flow?
options: It remains, creating an empty gap.
It is filled by other elements, as if the `absolute` element was never there.
It collapses, but only if the element has no content.
correctAnswer: It is filled by other elements, as if the `absolute` element was never there.
explanation: `absolute` elements are removed from the normal flow, so their original space is reclaimed by other elements.*

prompt: You are building a website header that should always be visible at the top of the browser window, even when the user scrolls down the page. Which `position` value should you apply to the header?
correctAnswer: `position: fixed;`
explanation: `position: fixed;` is the correct choice for elements that need to remain in a constant position relative to the viewport.*

prompt: For which `position` values does `z-index` have an effect?
correctAnswer: `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, `sticky`
explanation: `z-index` only applies to elements that are positioned (not `static`).*

prompt: What does a higher `z-index` value indicate for an overlapping element?
options: It will be placed behind elements with lower `z-index`.
It will be placed in front of elements with lower `z-index`.
It will have a larger width.
correctAnswer: It will be placed in front of elements with lower `z-index`.
explanation: Higher `z-index` values bring elements closer to the viewer.*

prompt: If two positioned elements overlap and neither has a `z-index` specified, which one will appear on top?
options: The one that appears first in the HTML document.
The one that appears last in the HTML document.
correctAnswer: The one that appears last in the HTML document.
explanation: In the absence of `z-index`, elements are stacked according to their order in the HTML document (later elements appear on top).*

prompt:
What is a
common beginner mistake when trying to use `z-index`?
correctAnswer: Applying it to `static` elements.
explanation: `z-index` only affects elements that have a `position` value other than `static`.*

prompt: What is a "stacking context" in CSS?
options: A property that defines the order of elements in the HTML.
A three-dimensional conceptualization of HTML elements along a Z-axis.
A method for aligning elements horizontally.
A way to group elements for styling purposes.
correctAnswer: A three-dimensional conceptualization of HTML elements along a Z-axis.

prompt: Which of the following properties can create a new stacking context, even if `position` is `static`?
correctAnswer: `opacity` less than 1
explanation: Properties like `opacity`, `transform`, and `filter` can establish new stacking contexts.*

prompt: If a child element has `z-index: 1000;` and its parent has `z-index: 10;`, but the parent is within a stacking context that is behind another element with `z-index: 5;`, what will happen?
options: The child element will appear on top of everything.
The child element will be stacked within its parent, and the parent's stacking context will determine its overall position.
The `z-index` of the child will override the parent.
correctAnswer: The child element will be stacked within its parent, and the parent's stacking context will determine its overall position.
explanation: A child's `z-index` is only relevant within its own stacking context. The parent's stacking context dictates its position relative to other contexts.*

prompt: You have a modal dialog that needs to appear on top of all other content. Which `position` and `z-index` combination is most appropriate for the modal?
correctAnswer: `position: fixed; z-index: 9999;`
explanation: `fixed` positions it relative to the viewport, and a high `z-index` ensures it's on top.*

prompt: When debugging `z-index` issues, you find an element with a very high `z-index` is still appearing behind another element with a lower `z-index`. What is the most likely reason?
options: The element with the lower `z-index` has a `background-color`.
The elements are in different stacking contexts, and the one appearing on top has a higher stacking context.
One of the elements has `display: inline;`.
correctAnswer: The elements are in different stacking contexts, and the one appearing on top has a higher stacking context.
explanation: This is a classic symptom of misunderstanding stacking contexts. The `z-index` only compares elements within the same stacking context.*

prompt: To ensure a dropdown menu always appears above its parent navigation item and other page content, what should be applied to the dropdown menu itself?
options: A `position` value other than `static` and a sufficiently high `z-index`.
correctAnswer: A `position` value other than `static` and a sufficiently high `z-index`.
explanation: The dropdown needs to be positioned (e.g., `absolute`) and given a `z-index` higher than its siblings and other elements it might overlap.*

prompt: What does the `overflow` property in CSS control?
options: How elements are positioned on the page.
What happens when content is too large to fit within an element's box.
correctAnswer: What happens when content is too large to fit within an element's box.
explanation: `overflow` manages content that exceeds its container's boundaries.*

prompt: Which `overflow` value is the default, causing content to spill out of its container?
correctAnswer: `visible`
explanation: `visible` is the default behavior, allowing content to render outside the element's box.*

prompt: If you want to hide any content that extends beyond an element's boundaries without providing scrollbars, which `overflow` value should you use?
correctAnswer: `hidden`
explanation: `overflow: hidden;` clips the content and prevents scrolling.*

prompt: Which `overflow` value adds scrollbars only when the content exceeds the container's dimensions?
correctAnswer: `auto`
explanation: `auto` provides scrollbars conditionally, improving user experience by only showing them when needed.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake related to `overflow` is:
options: Expecting `overflow: hidden;` to make content scrollable.
Not addressing content overflow, leading to layout breakage or overlapping elements.
Setting `overflow` on elements without a defined `width`.
correctAnswer: Not addressing content overflow, leading to layout breakage or overlapping elements.
explanation: Ignoring `overflow` can result in content spilling out and disrupting the design.*

prompt: You have a `div` with a fixed `height` and a lot of text content. You want users to be able to read all the text by scrolling within the `div`. Which `overflow` value should you apply?
correctAnswer: `overflow: scroll;` or `overflow: auto;`
explanation: Both `scroll` and `auto` enable scrolling. `auto` is generally preferred as it only shows scrollbars when necessary.*

prompt: Which CSS property can be used to control horizontal overflow specifically?
correctAnswer: `overflow-x`
explanation: `overflow-x` controls the horizontal overflow behavior.*

prompt: If an element has `overflow: hidden;` and contains an absolutely positioned child element that extends beyond its boundaries, what will happen to the child element?
options: The child element will be fully visible, ignoring the parent's `overflow`.
The child element will be clipped by the parent's boundaries.
The child element will cause the parent to show scrollbars.
The child element will be removed from the DOM.
correctAnswer: The child element will be clipped by the parent's boundaries.
explanation: Even absolutely positioned children are clipped by a parent with `overflow: hidden;`.*

prompt: For `overflow` to work as expected, what must typically be true about the element it's applied to?
options: It must have a defined `height` or `max-height`.
correctAnswer: It must have a defined `height` or `max-height`.
explanation: Without a constrained height, content will simply expand the element, and `overflow` won't trigger.*

prompt: You are creating a chat window with a fixed height. New messages are constantly added to the bottom. To ensure users can always see the latest messages, and scroll up to view older ones, which `overflow` setting is most appropriate for the message container?
correctAnswer: `overflow: scroll;` or `overflow: auto;`
explanation: `scroll` or `auto` on the `y` axis will allow vertical scrolling to view all messages within the fixed height.*

prompt: What does "intrinsic sizing" in CSS primarily refer to?
options: Setting fixed `width` and `height` values for elements.
How elements size themselves based on their content.
Using JavaScript to calculate element dimensions.
The default font size of an element.
correctAnswer: How elements size themselves based on their content.
explanation: Intrinsic sizing allows elements to adapt their dimensions based on their internal content.*

prompt: Which of the following elements typically has intrinsic dimensions by default?
correctAnswer: An `` tag without `width` or `height` attributes.
explanation: Images, by default, render at their natural pixel dimensions if not explicitly sized.*

prompt: If a `div` contains a very long word without spaces and its `width` is set to `min-content`, what will be the `div`'s width?
options: The width of the parent container.
The width of the longest word.
The smallest possible width without overflowing.
correctAnswer: The width of the longest word.
explanation: `min-content` will make the element just wide enough to contain its unbreakable content.*

prompt: Which `sizing` keyword makes an element as large as possible to fit all its content on a single line, preventing wrapping?
correctAnswer: `max-content`
explanation: `max-content` ensures all content is displayed without wrapping, making the element potentially very wide.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake related to intrinsic sizing is:
options: Forcing fixed `width` on content that should be fluid, causing overflow or responsiveness issues.
correctAnswer: Forcing fixed `width` on content that should be fluid, causing overflow or responsiveness issues.
explanation: Fighting against the natural flow of content by imposing rigid dimensions often leads to layout problems.*

prompt: You have a navigation item with text that varies in length. You want the item to be just wide enough to contain its text, but not wider than a certain maximum. Which `sizing` keyword would be most appropriate?
correctAnswer: `fit-content`
explanation: `fit-content` allows the element to grow up to `max-content` but not beyond the available space, then shrinks to `min-content` if needed.*

prompt: When an element has `width: auto;` and is a block-level element, what is its default behavior regarding width?
options: It shrinks to fit its content.
It takes up the full available width of its parent.
It inherits the width of its first child.
correctAnswer: It takes up the full available width of its parent.
explanation: Block-level elements with `width: auto;` typically expand to fill their parent's available horizontal space.*

prompt: Consider a `div` with `display: grid;` and a grid column defined as `grid-template-columns: min-content 1fr;`. What does `min-content` do for the first column?
options: It makes the column take up 100% of the available space.
It makes the column as narrow as possible without its content overflowing.
It makes the column as wide as possible to fit all its content on one line.
It sets the column to a fixed pixel width.
correctAnswer: It makes the column as narrow as possible without its content overflowing.
explanation: The `min-content` keyword ensures the column is only as wide as the widest unbreakable item within it.*

prompt: If you have a container with `display: flex;` and a child item with `flex-basis: max-content;`, what does this imply about the child's initial size?
options: It will try to take up all available space.
It will try to be as wide as its content allows, without wrapping.
It will be as small as possible without overflowing.
It will have a fixed width of `0px`.
correctAnswer: It will try to be as wide as its content allows, without wrapping.
explanation: `flex-basis: max-content;` tells the flex item to try and be as wide as its content's maximum intrinsic width.*

prompt: You are building a component where a sidebar should be just wide enough to accommodate its content (e.g., a list of links), and the main content area should take up the remaining space. Which CSS sizing approach would be most effective for the sidebar?
options: Setting a fixed `width` in `px` for the sidebar.
Applying `width: max-content;` or `width: fit-content;` to the sidebar within a flexible container.
correctAnswer: Applying `width: max-content;` or `width: fit-content;` to the sidebar within a flexible container.
explanation: `max-content` or `fit-content` allows the sidebar to naturally size to its content, while the main content can then use `flex-grow` or `1fr` to fill the rest.*

prompt: What is the most powerful tool for debugging CSS layout issues?
correctAnswer: The browser's Developer Tools (DevTools).
explanation: DevTools allow you to inspect the DOM, view applied styles, and experiment with changes in real-time.*

prompt: Which panel in the browser's DevTools is primarily used for inspecting HTML structure and CSS styles?
correctAnswer: Elements (or Inspector)
explanation: The Elements panel provides a visual representation of the DOM and the CSS rules applied to each element.*

prompt: What is a common beginner mistake when trying to fix a layout issue?
options: Using the browser's DevTools to inspect elements.
Randomly adding `margin`, `padding`, or `position: absolute;` without understanding the root cause.
Temporarily adding an `outline` to elements to see their boundaries.
Checking for typos in CSS class names.
correctAnswer: Randomly adding `margin`, `padding`, or `position: absolute;` without understanding the root cause.
explanation: "Guess and check" with spacing or positioning often creates more problems than it solves and leads to fragile code.*

prompt: What is the purpose of the "outline trick" (`* { outline: 1px solid red; }`) in layout debugging?
options: To permanently style all elements with a red border.
To visually reveal the boundaries of every element, making it easier to spot overflow or sizing issues.
To improve the performance of the page.
correctAnswer: To visually reveal the boundaries of every element, making it easier to spot overflow or sizing issues.
explanation: Outlines provide a clear visual map of the layout structure without affecting the document flow.*

prompt: You notice an unexpected horizontal scrollbar on your page. What is a likely cause?
options: An element's total width (content + padding + border + margin) exceeds the viewport width.
correctAnswer: An element's total width (content + padding + border + margin) exceeds the viewport width.
explanation: Horizontal scrolling usually occurs when an element is wider than its container or the viewport.*

prompt: When inspecting an element in DevTools, you see a CSS rule crossed out. What does this indicate?
options: The rule is invalid CSS syntax.
The rule has been overridden by a more specific rule or one that appears later in the cascade.
The rule is not supported by the browser.
The rule is causing a layout error.
correctAnswer: The rule has been overridden by a more specific rule or one that appears later in the cascade.
explanation: Crossed-out rules are valid but are not currently applied because another rule has higher priority.*

prompt: You have two paragraphs, and the space between them is smaller than the sum of their vertical margins. What CSS concept is likely at play?
correctAnswer: Margin collapse
explanation: Margin collapse causes adjacent vertical margins to merge into a single margin.*

prompt: An element with `position: absolute;` is appearing in an unexpected location on the page. What should you check first?
options: The `position` property of its ancestor elements to find its containing block.
correctAnswer: The `position` property of its ancestor elements to find its containing block.
explanation: Absolutely positioned elements are placed relative to their nearest positioned ancestor. If none exists, they position relative to the initial containing block.*

prompt: You want to see how an element's layout changes when it is hovered over, but moving your mouse away removes the hover state. How can you debug this in DevTools?
options: You cannot debug hover states in DevTools.
Use the "Force state" feature (e.g., `:hover`) in the Elements panel to simulate the hover state.
correctAnswer: Use the "Force state" feature (e.g., `:hover`) in the Elements panel to simulate the hover state.
explanation: DevTools allows you to force pseudo-classes like `:hover`, `:active`, and `:focus` to inspect their styles.*

prompt: When using the "outline trick", why is `outline` preferred over `border`?
options: `outline` does not take up space in the box model and therefore does not affect the layout itself.
`outline` can be applied to more elements than `border`.
correctAnswer: `outline` does not take up space in the box model and therefore does not affect the layout itself.
explanation: Because `outline` is drawn outside the element's dimensions, it won't cause elements to shift or wrap, which `border` might do.*

prompt: What CSS property is used to create a flex container?
correctAnswer: `display: flex;`
explanation: Applying `display: flex;` or `display: inline-flex;` to a parent element turns it into a flex container.*

prompt: Once an element becomes a flex container, what do its direct children automatically become?
correctAnswer: Flex items
explanation: Direct children of a flex container are automatically treated as flex items.*

prompt: Which of the following properties are ignored by direct children of a flex container?
correctAnswer: `float`
explanation: `float`, `clear`, and `vertical-align` have no effect on flex items.*

prompt: What is the primary purpose of a flex container?
options: To define the font size of its children.
To distribute space among its items and align them in one dimension.
To add a border around its children.
To change the background color of its children.
correctAnswer: To distribute space among its items and align them in one dimension.
explanation: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for distributing space and aligning items.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake when working with Flexbox is:
options: Forgetting to set `width` on flex items.
Applying Flexbox properties to flex items before making their parent a flex container.
correctAnswer: Applying Flexbox properties to flex items before making their parent a flex container.
explanation: Flex item properties only work when their parent is a flex container.*

prompt: If you apply `display: inline-flex;` to an element, how will it behave?
options: It will behave like a block-level flex container.
It will behave like an inline-level flex container, flowing with text.
It will behave like a grid container.
It will not create a flex formatting context.
correctAnswer: It will behave like an inline-level flex container, flowing with text.
explanation: `inline-flex` creates a flex container that itself behaves like an inline element.*

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a property that can be applied directly to a flex container?
correctAnswer: `align-self`
explanation: `align-self` is a property applied to individual flex items, not the container.*

prompt:
What is the
relationship between a flex container and its direct children?
options: The children become flex items and their layout is controlled by the flex container's properties.
The children inherit all properties from the flex container.
The children are removed from the document flow.
correctAnswer: The children become flex items and their layout is controlled by the flex container's properties.
explanation: The flex container dictates how its direct children (flex items) are laid out and aligned.*

prompt: When a parent element is declared as a flex container, what happens to the `margin` properties of its direct children?
options: They still work as expected, but margin collapse is prevented.
correctAnswer: They still work as expected, but margin collapse is prevented.
explanation: Margins on flex items are respected, and margin collapse does not occur between adjacent flex items.*

prompt: You have a `div` containing three `img` elements. To arrange these images in a row with equal spacing between them, what is the first step you should take?
options: Set a fixed `width` on each `img` element.
correctAnswer: Apply `display: flex;` to the parent `div`.
explanation: Making the parent `div` a flex container is the essential first step to enable Flexbox layout for its image children.*

prompt: What CSS property on the flex container determines the direction of the main axis?
correctAnswer: `flex-direction`
explanation: `flex-direction` sets the primary direction of item arrangement, thus defining the main axis.*

prompt: If `flex-direction` is set to `row`, in which direction does the main axis run?
correctAnswer: Horizontally
explanation: `row` means items are arranged from left to right (or right to left with `row-reverse`), making the main axis horizontal.*

prompt: If the main axis runs vertically, in which direction does the cross axis run?
correctAnswer: Horizontally
explanation: The cross axis is always perpendicular to the main axis.*

prompt: Which Flexbox property is used to align flex items along the main axis?
correctAnswer: `justify-content`
explanation: `justify-content` distributes space and aligns items along the main axis.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake when using Flexbox is:
options: Forgetting to set `display: flex;` on the container.
Confusing the main and cross axes, leading to incorrect alignment property usage.
correctAnswer: Confusing the main and cross axes, leading to incorrect alignment property usage.
explanation: Misunderstanding which axis is which often leads to using `justify-content` when `align-items` is needed, or vice versa.*

prompt: You have a flex container with `flex-direction: column;`. Which property would you use to vertically center the flex items?
correctAnswer: `justify-content: center;`
explanation: When `flex-direction: column;`, the main axis is vertical, so `justify-content` controls vertical alignment.*

prompt: With `flex-direction: row;`, which property would you use to horizontally center the flex items?
correctAnswer: `justify-content: center;`
explanation: When `flex-direction: row;`, the main axis is horizontal, so `justify-content` controls horizontal alignment.*

prompt: If a flex container has `flex-direction: row;`, which property would you use to vertically align the flex items?
correctAnswer: `align-items`
explanation: With a horizontal main axis, the cross axis is vertical, and `align-items` controls alignment along the cross axis.*

prompt: Consider a flex container with `flex-direction: column;`. Which property would you use to horizontally align the flex items?
correctAnswer: `align-items`
explanation: With a vertical main axis, the cross axis is horizontal, and `align-items` controls alignment along the cross axis.*

prompt: You are building a navigation bar where links should be evenly spaced horizontally and vertically centered. What `flex-direction` and alignment properties would you likely use on the navigation container?
correctAnswer: `flex-direction: row; justify-content: space-around; align-items: center;`
explanation: `flex-direction: row;` for horizontal layout, `justify-content: space-around;` for even horizontal spacing, and `align-items: center;` for vertical centering.*

prompt: Which Flexbox property aligns flex items along the main axis?
correctAnswer: `justify-content`
explanation: `justify-content` specifically handles alignment and space distribution along the main axis.*

prompt: To which element is the `justify-content` property applied?
correctAnswer: The flex container.
explanation: `justify-content` is a container property that affects all its direct flex item children.*

prompt: Which `justify-content` value distributes items evenly, with the first item at the start and the last item at the end of the main axis?
correctAnswer: `space-between`
explanation: `space-between` maximizes the space between items while anchoring the first and last.*

prompt: If you want to center all flex items horizontally within a `flex-direction: row;` container, which `justify-content` value would you use?
correctAnswer: `center`
explanation: `center` aligns items to the middle of the main axis.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake when using `justify-content` is:
options: Expecting it to align items along the cross axis.
Forgetting to set `display: flex;` on the container.
correctAnswer: Expecting it to align items along the cross axis.
explanation: `justify-content` is strictly for the main axis; `align-items` is for the cross axis.*

prompt: Which `justify-content` value ensures that the space between any two items, and the space to the edges of the container, is equal?
correctAnswer: `space-evenly`
explanation: `space-evenly` provides perfectly equal spacing across the entire main axis.*

prompt: You have a navigation bar with `display: flex;` and `flex-direction: row;`. You want the navigation links to be pushed to the right side of the bar. Which `justify-content` value should you use?
correctAnswer: `flex-end`
explanation: `flex-end` aligns items to the end of the main axis, which is the right side in a `row` direction.*

prompt: What is the default value of `justify-content`?
correctAnswer: `flex-start`
explanation: By default, flex items are packed towards the beginning of the main axis.*

prompt: If a flex container has `flex-direction: column;`, and you apply `justify-content: space-between;`, how will the items be spaced?
options: Evenly spaced vertically, with the first item at the top and the last at the bottom.
correctAnswer: Evenly spaced vertically, with the first item at the top and the last at the bottom.
explanation: When `flex-direction: column;`, the main axis is vertical, so `justify-content` controls vertical spacing.*

prompt: You are building a card layout where each row contains three cards. You want the cards to be evenly distributed across the row, with some space at the beginning and end, but less space than between the cards. Which `justify-content` value would best achieve this?
correctAnswer: `space-around`
explanation: `space-around` creates equal space around each item, resulting in half the space at the ends compared to between items.*

prompt: Which Flexbox property aligns flex items along the cross axis?
correctAnswer: `align-items`
explanation: `align-items` specifically handles alignment perpendicular to the main axis.*

prompt: To which element is the `align-items` property applied?
correctAnswer: The flex container.
explanation: `align-items` is a container property that affects all its direct flex item children.*

prompt: If a flex container has `flex-direction: row;`, which `align-items` value would vertically center the flex items?
correctAnswer: `center`
explanation: When the main axis is horizontal (`row`), the cross axis is vertical, so `center` aligns items vertically.*

prompt: What is the default value of `align-items`?
correctAnswer: `stretch`
explanation: By default, flex items stretch to fill the container along the cross axis.*

prompt: A common beginner mistake when using `align-items` is:
options: Expecting it to align items along the main axis.
Forgetting to set `display: flex;` on the container.
correctAnswer: Expecting it to align items along the main axis.
explanation: `align-items` is strictly for the cross axis; `justify-content` is for the main axis.*

prompt: You have a flex container with `flex-direction: column;`. Which `align-items` value would horizontally center the flex items?
correctAnswer: `center`
explanation: When the main axis is vertical (`column`), the cross axis is horizontal, so `center` aligns items horizontally.*

prompt: Which `align-items` value aligns flex items such that their baselines align?
correctAnswer: `baseline`
explanation: `baseline` is useful for aligning text content across different flex items.*

prompt: If a flex item has a fixed `height` (e.g., `height: 100px;`), and its flex container has `align-items: stretch;`, what will be the actual height of that flex item?
options: It will stretch to fill the container.
correctAnswer: It will remain `100px`.
explanation: `stretch` only works if the item does not have a fixed dimension along the cross axis.*

prompt: You are creating a header with a logo on the left and navigation links on the right. You want both the logo and links to be vertically centered within the header. Assuming `flex-direction: row;` on the header, which property should you use?
correctAnswer: `align-items: center;`
explanation: `align-items: center;` will vertically center the items along the cross axis when the main axis is horizontal.*

prompt: Consider a flex container with `flex-direction: column;`. You want all flex items to start at the top of the container. Which `align-items` value should you use?
correctAnswer: `flex-start`
explanation: `flex-start` aligns items to the beginning of the cross axis.
